Experiment 4 (stimulus variance SD 3/5/7): a walkthrough of the results

Regression to the mean in perceptual experience — exploratory, not the main write-up

19 September 2026

About this document

Experiment 4 - stimulus variance (SD 3/5/7). Arrays of 10 coloured squares whose colours were spread around the mean with SD 3, 5 or 7 (72 trials per level, 216 per session). Only the within-array spread changes; this is the clean noise manipulation. Participants reported the colour on a 50-step scale, either the average colour or how red/blue the array felt (experience condition).

This document walks through every result of this experiment: first whether the data and the manipulation are sound, then what they show about regression to the mean (RttM) in perceptual experience. Every number and figure is recomputed from the analysis pipeline when the file is knitted; it is exploratory and not part of the main write-up. True values are the mean of the squares actually shown (EPOC_TRUE_VALUE = "shown").

Two directions of RttM. Forward: given a stimulus, is the report less extreme? (slope of report on true value). Reverse: given a report, was the stimulus less extreme? (the exaggeration claim: extreme experiences overstate the world). Pure noise produces reverse RttM but leaves the forward slope at 1, so a forward slope below 1 needs more than noise.

Bottom line

The clean test, and it supports both directions of the account. Tracking falls (r .83 / .78 / .71) and the forward slope drops from 1.08 to 0.94 to 0.82 (strict model p < .001; survives trial order, value reweighting and participant-level testing). About 58% of the drop is noise (the weaker correlation) and 42% a genuine narrowing of the reports (p < .001), which noise alone cannot produce. Extreme reports come from less extreme stimuli at every level (reverse slope about .6), and more so at higher noise: reports of the same extreme stimulus were pulled 1.8–2.4 units further toward the middle at SD 7 than at SD 3; and for the same extreme report the stimulus was 0.6–1.0 unit less extreme at SD 7 than at SD 3 (high reports as given; both tails once each participant’s shift is removed), in the same direction at both ends, which is the signature of more exaggeration rather than a shift. Average and experience conditions do not differ.

Key results at a glance (levels in order of increasing noise)
Question Result

Does the forward slope change with noise? (strict model) slopes 1.08 / 0.94 / 0.82; p < .001
Same, participant-level ANOVA p < .001
Do reports narrow at higher noise (SD ratio, lowest vs highest level)? ratio 1.36 / 1.25 / 1.21; p < .001

Same extreme low report: stimulus less extreme at SD 7 than SD 3? (shift removed) +0.67 units, p = .003

1. Sample and data quality

Participant flow
Stage Average Experience
Started 53 58
Second session (already did the other condition) 0 1
Incomplete session 0 0
Kept < 85% of trials 2 2
Did not track the stimulus (Spearman r ≤ .30) 0 5
Analysed 51 50
  • Trials analysed: average 10,603 (about 208 per participant, mean absolute error 4.42 units); experience 10,475 (about 210 per participant, mean absolute error 4.51 units).
  • Cleaning, identical for all experiments: second sessions dropped; reports of 0 treated as missing (the response scale’s starting value, saved when someone clicks without crossing the scale); RT < 200 ms or > 8 s; ±2.5 SD RT trimming per participant; errors ≥ 30 units; participants keeping < 85% of trials or with Spearman r ≤ .30.

2. Does the manipulation work?

Stimulus checks (true value = mean of the squares shown)
Level Spread within arrays (SD) Spread of true means (SD) Mean true value
SD 3 2.86 6.28 24.14
SD 5 4.75 6.20 24.19
SD 7 6.65 6.23 24.69

The spread of true means across trials is the same at every level, so only the arrays themselves differ between levels. At a fixed true mean, the make-up of an array does not predict the report; adding it changes the slopes by at most 0.002.

Problems found.

  1. The trial list is not properly shuffled (confirmed in colorvariance/index.html): both the SD-level list and the true-value list were built in order and ‘shuffled’ with .sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5), which leaves items near their starting place. SD 3 trials come earlier in each block and SD 7 later, and SD 3 received slightly more low true values, SD 7 more high ones. Both are controlled below (trial position; reweighting).
  2. The top of the value range was cut: 115 values (14–36) were built and the first 108 kept before shuffling, so 35 appears less often and 36 never.
  3. One-step colour offset between stimulus squares and response images: a square of value p matches response index p − 1, so a perfect observer would report about 1 unit low. No effect on slopes, correlations or comparisons between levels.
  4. The logged true value is the rounded target; the squares shown differ by at most ±0.3 at random.

Compression shows up as positive values at both ends (reports move toward the middle from both sides); opposite signs at the two ends mean an overall shift of the reports at one level rather than compression.

5. Why the forward slope changes: noise and narrowing

Slope = correlation × (SD of reports / SD of true values); values centred within participant
Level Within-array SD r SD true SD reports SD ratio Slope Calibrated slope (r²) Reverse slope
SD 3 2.86 0.799 6.28 8.53 1.36 1.08 0.64 0.59
SD 5 4.75 0.749 6.20 7.76 1.25 0.94 0.56 0.60
SD 7 6.65 0.678 6.23 7.50 1.21 0.82 0.46 0.56

From SD 3 to SD 7: log change in slope -0.283, of which 58% from the correlation and 42% from the SD ratio (within participants: correlation p < .001, ratio p < .001). Pure noise would raise the ratio as the correlation falls; a falling ratio is a genuine narrowing of the reports. A calibrated observer’s forward slope would equal r²; slopes above that mean people correct less than their noise warrants, which leaves extreme reports exaggerated (reverse slope = r² / forward slope).

Average true value behind each report value, all levels (reports as given)

Lowest vs highest level, each participant’s constant shift removed

How much more the same extreme report exaggerated its stimulus at SD 7 than at SD 3 (positive = more exaggeration at the higher level)
Extreme reports Participant-level + trial position + position, reweighted
High (≥ 36) as given +0.88, p < .001 +0.92, p < .001 +1.00, p < .001
Low (≤ 14) as given +0.33, p = .249 +0.24, p = .391 +0.09, p = .759

Low (≤ 14) shift removed +0.67, p = .003 +0.59, p = .009 +0.44, p = .047

Only trials with the same report value are compared. “Shift removed” subtracts each participant’s average reporting error at each level first, so a general tendency to answer high or low at one level cannot look like exaggeration at one end; it removes only a constant, not the regression itself. “Reweighted” gives every level the same distribution of true values.

The absolute size of the gap depends on the range of stimuli presented (true values here span about 14–36), so it describes observer and stimulus set together; the differences between levels, which share the same stimulus distribution, carry the claim.
